extracted.intended_audience: citizens of New York; engaged electorate; readers interested in constitutional government and the Articles of Confederation
extracted.subtask_description: A close argumentative examination of the structural defects of a confederation (the Articles of Confederation) and the constitutional powers needed in a national government to ensure unity, security, and effective administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total want of a SANCTION to its laws
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States, as now composed, have no powers to exact obedience, or punish disobedience to their resolutions, either by pecuniary mulcts, by a suspension or divestiture of privileges, or by any other constitutional mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the dilemma created by the reservation clause (powers not expressly delegated remain with states) and why the absence of an express enforcement power renders the Confederation unable to enforce its laws; examples of possible sanctions are listed (fines, suspension/divestiture of privileges, use of force).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual guaranty of State governments
rubrics_metrics.description: The want of a mutual guaranty of the State governments is another capital imperfection in the federal plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A guaranty would permit the Union to assist in repelling domestic dangers (usurpation, faction, sedition) and protect state constitutions against violent change; it would not impede lawful, popular reforms. Cites Massachusetts' convulsions as proof domestic dangers are real.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority for the national government to raise its own revenues
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no method of steering clear of this inconvenience, but by authorizing the national government to raise its own revenues in its own way. Imposts, excises, and, in general, all duties upon articles of consumption ... must for a long time constitute the chief part of the revenue raised in this country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues quotas/requisitions are impracticable and unequal; recommends indirect taxes (consumption duties) because they 'find their level' and self-limit; acknowledges direct taxes may require apportionment by population but are harder to value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of quotas/requisitions as a sound fiscal principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of regulating the contributions of the States to the common treasury by QUOTAS is another fundamental error in the Confederation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that no common standard (land value or population) reliably measures a state's ability to pay; quotas produce glaring inequality and oppression and invite enforcement by force in some cases. Historical parallels and comparisons to provinces/counties illustrate impossibility of fair quota rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer indirect taxes (duties on consumption) as stable revenue sources
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a signal advantage of taxes on articles of consumption, that they contain in their own nature a security against excess. They prescribe their own limit; which cannot be exceeded without defeating the end proposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains the self-limiting mechanism (high duties reduce consumption and revenue); argues indirect taxes will likely form chief part of national revenue and help avoid private oppression; notes that different states' inequalities may be counterbalanced across various duties over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical rule for apportioning direct taxes (use numbers)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a branch of taxation where no limits to the discretion of the government are to be found in the nature of things, the establishment of a fixed rule, not incompatible with the end, may be attended with fewer inconveniences ... numbers, in the view of simplicity and certainty, are entitled to a preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges direct taxes (land/buildings) might admit apportionment; but land valuation is costly and impractical in an unsettled country, so population counts (numbers) are preferable for simplicity and certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to regulate commerce vested in the national government
rubrics_metrics.description: The want of a power to regulate commerce is by all parties allowed to be of the number. ... there is no object, either as it respects the interests of trade or finance, that more strongly demands a federal superintendence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues national regulation of commerce is essential for effective treaties, preventing inter-state conflicts and clashing regulations that impede trade (examples: German principalities' duties, separate State prohibitions). Without it, foreign powers will exploit disunity in treaty-making and markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: National authority to raise and maintain armies (not mere requisitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of raising armies, by the most obvious construction of the articles of the Confederation, is merely a power of making requisitions upon the States for quotas of men. This practice ... was found replete with obstructions to a vigorous and to an economical system of defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains requisitions caused competition and auctions for recruits (high bounties), short enlistments, frequent fluctuations, and unequal burdens among states; recommends national power to raise troops to ensure discipline, economy, and consistent defense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition to equal suffrage among unequal States
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of equal suffrage among the States is another exceptionable part of the Confederation. Every idea of proportion and every rule of fair representation conspire to condemn a principle, which gives ... an equal weight in the scale of power with ... much larger states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues one-state-one-vote violates principles of republican government by allowing small states to overrule larger populations; warns that larger states will eventually revolt from such privation of political importance and that equal suffrage distorts justice and common-sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of excessive requirement for unanimity or supermajorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of unanimity in public bodies, or of something approaching towards it, has been founded upon a supposition that it would contribute to security. But its real operation is to embarrass the administration, to destroy the energy of the government ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Details practical harms: delays, negotiation, intrigues, compromises of public good, and incapacity to act in emergencies; shows how foreign powers can more easily corrupt smaller required majorities than larger simple majorities; gives war/peace and commerce examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection against foreign corruption and influence
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not difficult to discover, that a principle of this kind gives greater scope to foreign corruption, as well as to domestic faction, than that which permits the sense of the majority to decide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses historical examples (United Provinces, Sweden) to show deputies or princes were bought by foreign emissaries; argues broad, workable majorities and robust national institutions reduce vulnerability to bribery and external manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establishment of a national judiciary / supreme tribunal
rubrics_metrics.description: A circumstance which crowns the defects of the Confederation remains yet to be mentioned, the want of a judiciary power. Laws are a dead letter without courts to expound and define their true meaning and operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues treaties and national laws require uniform interpretation by a supreme tribunal instituted under the same authority that forms treaties; without it, multiple final determinations by state courts would produce endless diversity and legal uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid substituting violence (the sword) for lawful magistracy
rubrics_metrics.description: A sovereignty over sovereigns, a government over governments, a legislation for communities, as contradistinguished from individuals, ... in practice it is subversive of the order and ends of civil polity, by substituting VIOLENCE in place of LAW, or the destructive COERCION of the SWORD in place of the mild and salutary COERCION of the MAGISTRACY.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns that defective constitutions tempt the use or usurpation of force; endorses constitutional delegation of proper powers to national magistracy to preserve order without arbitrary violence; draws lesson from historical confederacies that required extraordinary assumptions of power in crises.
